title: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
description: Class 12 Economics: the state of the Indian economy under British rule — colonial exploitation, stagnant agriculture, de-industrialisation, foreign trade, occupational structure, demography and infrastructure.

topics.title: Colonial Rule and the Agricultural Sector
topics.concept:
When India became independent in 1947, it inherited an economy shattered by nearly two centuries of British colonial rule. The sole aim of British policy had been to serve the interests of Britain — India was used as a supplier of cheap raw materials for British industry and a market for finished British goods. As a result, India's own economy was kept backward and stagnant.

By the eve of independence, India's economy showed the marks of this colonial exploitation: very low growth (national income grew at well under 1% a year in the first half of the 20th century), low per-capita income, and widespread poverty.

The agricultural sector — on which about 85% of the population depended — was in a particularly poor state. Its key features:

  • It was stagnant and backward, with very low productivity. Farming used old methods and there was little irrigation or modern technology.
  • The land revenue (zamindari) system in many areas left actual cultivators poor and exploited, while intermediaries (zamindars) profited; this killed any incentive to improve the land.
  • Farmers were forced into commercialisation of agriculture — growing cash crops (like indigo and cotton) for export rather than food for themselves — which often caused hardship and famine.
  • Output was low and the country could not even feed itself well; famines were common.

So at independence, the foundation of the economy — agriculture — was weak, low in productivity, and structured to benefit Britain rather than the Indian farmer.

examples.problem: Example 1: What was the main aim of British economic policy in India?
examples.solution:
It served Britain.

  • To use India as a supplier of cheap raw materials and a market for British finished goods.
examples.answer: To serve Britain — using India as a supplier of cheap raw materials and a market for British finished goods.

examples.problem: Example 2: Why was Indian agriculture stagnant under British rule?
examples.solution:
Low productivity and bad systems.

  • Old methods, little irrigation/technology, low productivity.
  • The zamindari system left cultivators poor with no incentive to improve land.
examples.answer: Because of low productivity, old methods, little irrigation, and the exploitative zamindari land-revenue system that gave cultivators no incentive to improve.

examples.problem: Example 3: What is meant by the 'commercialisation' of agriculture under the British?
examples.solution:
Cash crops for export.

  • Farmers were made to grow cash crops (like indigo, cotton) for export.
  • Rather than food for their own use, which often caused hardship.
examples.answer: Forcing farmers to grow cash crops for export (e.g. indigo, cotton) instead of food, which often caused hardship and famine.

recap:
• India became independent in 1947 with an economy weakened by colonial rule aimed at serving Britain (raw materials supplier + market for British goods).
  • Marks of exploitation: low growth (<1%/yr), low per-capita income, poverty.
  • Agriculture (~85% of people): stagnant, low productivity, exploitative zamindari system, forced commercialisation (cash crops), famines.

quiz.q: Under British rule, India was mainly used as a supplier of:
quiz.explanation: India supplied cheap raw materials and was a market for British goods.

quiz.q: At independence, about what share of people depended on agriculture?
quiz.explanation: Around 85% of the population depended on agriculture.

topics.title: De-industrialisation, Foreign Trade and Occupational Structure
topics.concept:
The British did not just neglect industry — their policies actively de-industrialised India. Before colonial rule, India was famous for its handicrafts (fine textiles, metalwork) that were known worldwide. Under the British, these were systematically ruined:

  • Cheap, machine-made British goods (especially textiles) flooded Indian markets and destroyed the demand for Indian handicrafts.
  • India's traditional handicraft industries declined, throwing artisans out of work, while no modern industry was built to replace them. This twin process — the decline of handicrafts without the rise of modern industry — is called de-industrialisation.
  • A few modern industries (cotton textiles in the west, jute in the east, later iron and steel — TISCO, 1907) did come up, but they were too few, concentrated in a few regions, and largely under foreign control. There was almost no capital goods industry.

India's foreign trade was shaped to benefit Britain: India became an exporter of primary products (raw cotton, jute, indigo, tea, food grains) and an importer of finished goods (British cloth, machinery). India usually had an export surplus, but this did not help Indians — it was used to pay for Britain's expenses and led to a drain of wealth from India to Britain.

The occupational structure hardly changed throughout British rule: agriculture employed about 70–75% of the workforce, while industry and services together employed only a small share. This showed an undeveloped, backward economy that had failed to modernise.

examples.problem: Example 1: What is meant by 'de-industrialisation' of India under British rule?
examples.solution:
Handicrafts ruined, no modern industry.

  • The decline of India's traditional handicraft industries.
  • Without the rise of any modern industry to replace them.
examples.answer: The decline of India's traditional handicrafts without the growth of modern industry to replace them.

examples.problem: Example 2: Describe the nature of India's foreign trade under the British.
examples.solution:
Raw materials out, finished goods in.

  • India exported primary products (raw cotton, jute, tea) and imported finished goods.
  • The export surplus was used for British expenses — a drain of wealth.
examples.answer: India exported primary products and imported finished goods; the export surplus financed Britain's expenses (a drain of wealth).

examples.problem: Example 3: Why did India's occupational structure show a backward economy?
examples.solution:
Too many in agriculture.

  • About 70–75% of the workforce was in agriculture.
  • Very few in industry/services — a sign of an undeveloped economy.
examples.answer: Because about 70–75% of workers were stuck in low-productivity agriculture with few in industry or services — a mark of an undeveloped economy.

recap:
• De-industrialisation: British machine goods ruined India's famous handicrafts, with no modern industry to replace them; few modern factories (jute, cotton, TISCO 1907), foreign-controlled.
  • Foreign trade: exporter of raw materials, importer of finished goods; export surplus → drain of wealth to Britain.
  • Occupational structure: ~70–75% in agriculture, little change — an undeveloped economy.

quiz.q: The ruin of India's handicrafts without modern industry replacing them is called:
Under British rule, India mainly exported:
quiz.explanation: India exported raw materials and imported finished goods.

topics.title: Demographic Condition and Infrastructure
topics.concept:
The demographic condition of India before independence was typical of a poor, underdeveloped country (the "first stage" of demographic transition):

  • Both the birth rate and the death rate were very high (around 48 and 40 per thousand). High death rates were caused by famines, epidemics and lack of healthcare.
  • Life expectancy was extremely low — only about 32 years.
  • Infant mortality was very high (about 218 per thousand), and overall literacy was very low — under 16%, with female literacy near 7%.
  • Mass poverty and poor health and education were the rule.

The infrastructure that the British did build was meant to serve their own interests, not India's development:

  • Railways (introduced in 1853) were the most important. They did break India's isolation and help movement — but their main purpose was to carry raw materials from the interior to the ports for export, and British goods inland; they were not built to develop India.
  • Roads, ports, and the telegraph were similarly developed for British administration and trade.
  • There was very little development of schools, hospitals, irrigation or modern industry — the things that would have helped ordinary Indians.

So on the eve of independence, India was a backward, stagnant economy — poor agriculture, ruined handicrafts, little industry, a drained treasury, a high-birth-high-death population, mass illiteracy, and an infrastructure built for the coloniser. This was the difficult starting point from which independent India had to build its development — the subject of the chapters that follow.

examples.problem: Example 1: Describe the demographic condition of India on the eve of independence.
examples.solution:
High birth & death, low life expectancy.

  • Very high birth and death rates; very low life expectancy (~32 years).
  • High infant mortality and very low literacy (under 16%).
examples.answer: Very high birth and death rates, low life expectancy (~32 years), high infant mortality, and very low literacy (under 16%).

examples.problem: Example 2: What was the real purpose of the railways built by the British?
examples.solution:
To serve British trade.

  • Mainly to carry raw materials to ports for export and British goods inland.
  • Not to develop India.
examples.answer: Mainly to move raw materials to ports for export and British goods inland — to serve British trade, not India's development.

examples.problem: Example 3: Why is it said British infrastructure was built for British interests?
examples.solution:
It served trade and administration, not people.

  • Railways, roads, ports and telegraph served British trade and rule.
  • Schools, hospitals and irrigation for Indians were neglected.
examples.answer: Because railways, roads, ports and the telegraph served British trade and administration, while schools, hospitals and irrigation for Indians were neglected.

recap:
• Demography: high birth & death rates, life expectancy ~32 years, high infant mortality, literacy <16% — a poor, underdeveloped country.
  • Infrastructure (railways 1853, roads, ports, telegraph) built for British interests (move raw materials to ports), not India's development; schools/hospitals/irrigation neglected.
  • Independent India inherited a backward, stagnant economy.

quiz.q: Life expectancy in India on the eve of independence was about:
quiz.explanation: Life expectancy was only about 32 years.

quiz.q: The railways built by the British were mainly meant to:
options: Carry raw materials to ports for export
quiz.explanation: Their main purpose was to serve British trade (move raw materials to ports).

questions.explanation: India became independent in 1947.

questions.explanation: British policy served Britain's interests.

questions.q: Under the British, India was a supplier of ____ and a market for British finished goods.
questions.explanation: India supplied cheap raw materials.

questions.explanation: Around 85% depended on agriculture.

questions.q: The exploitative land-revenue system that left cultivators poor was the:
questions.explanation: The zamindari system exploited cultivators.

questions.q: Forcing farmers to grow cash crops for export is the ____ of agriculture.
questions.explanation: Growing cash crops for export is commercialisation.

questions.q: The decline of handicrafts without modern industry replacing them is:
questions.explanation: That twin process is de-industrialisation.

questions.q: India's first iron and steel company (TISCO) was set up in:
questions.explanation: TISCO was established in 1907.

questions.q: Under British rule, India mainly exported:
questions.explanation: India exported raw materials and imported finished goods.

questions.q: The export surplus that went to pay Britain's expenses is called the:
questions.explanation: This is the drain of wealth from India to Britain.

questions.q: About what share of the workforce was in agriculture under British rule?
questions.explanation: Around 70–75% of workers were in agriculture.

questions.q: Life expectancy on the eve of independence was about:
questions.explanation: Life expectancy was only about 32 years.

questions.q: The literacy rate at independence was under:
questions.explanation: Literacy was under 16%.

questions.q: Railways were introduced in India in:
questions.explanation: Railways were introduced in 1853.

questions.q: British infrastructure was mainly built to serve:
questions.explanation: It served British trade and administration, not India's development.

questions.q: Indian-made textiles, once exported worldwide, lost their markets under the British mainly because:
options: Cheap machine-made British cloth flooded India
questions.explanation: Machine-made British imports undercut and destroyed the handicraft textile industry — de-industrialisation.

questions.q: Although India often ran an export surplus under the British, ordinary Indians did not benefit because the surplus was used to:
options: Meet Britain's expenses (a drain of wealth)
questions.explanation: The surplus financed colonial expenses, draining resources out of India rather than developing it.

questions.q: The near-unchanged occupational structure (most people in agriculture for decades) indicates that the economy was:
questions.explanation: A workforce stuck in agriculture, with no shift to industry/services, signals an undeveloped, stagnant economy.

questions.q: Both high birth and high death rates with very low life expectancy place colonial India in the demographic stage typical of a:
questions.explanation: High birth and death rates and ~32-year life expectancy are hallmarks of an underdeveloped economy.

questions.q: The railways are described as a 'mixed blessing' because they:
options: Helped movement and broke isolation, but were built mainly to serve British trade
questions.explanation: They modernised transport yet were designed to move raw materials to ports for export, serving Britain first.

questions.q: The commercialisation of agriculture sometimes worsened famines because farmers grew:
options: Cash crops for export instead of food for themselves
questions.explanation: Shifting land from food to export cash crops reduced food availability, deepening hunger in bad years.

questions.q: A key reason Indian agriculture stayed low in productivity was the zamindari system, which gave cultivators:
options: No incentive to improve the land they did not own
questions.explanation: Tenants who handed most produce to intermediaries had little reason or means to invest in the land.

questions.q: The few modern industries that did develop (jute, cotton, steel) were limited because they were:
options: Few, regionally concentrated and largely foreign-controlled, with no capital-goods base
questions.explanation: Sparse, concentrated and foreign-dominated industry, lacking machine-making capacity, could not modernise the economy.

questions.q: Independent India in 1947 inherited an economy best described as:
options: Backward and stagnant, needing planned development
questions.explanation: Weak agriculture, ruined crafts, little industry and mass poverty made planned development the urgent task.

questions.q: Studying the eve of independence matters because it explains why independent India chose to focus on:
options: Self-reliance, industry and agricultural reform through planning
questions.explanation: The colonial damage shaped India's post-1947 priorities: planning, industrialisation, food security and self-reliance.
